newsitem.title: USA: Sears backs away from Mexico in shift to U.S. focus.
newsitem.headline: Sears backs away from Mexico in shift to U.S. focus.

text.p: Sears Roebuck and Co. backed away from its lagging Mexican business Wednesday, agreeing to sell most of it for $103 million to Grupo Carso SA de CV, the largest conglomerate in Latin America.
Controlled by Mexican billionaire Carlos Slim, Carso is a successful turn-around specialist, analysts said.

"Sears of Mexico has not been a stellar performer," said Bear Stearns retailing analyst Santiago Pique in New York. "This is what Carso does -- it buys companies that are under-performing or under-managed and turns them around."
Sears Mexico has 45 stores and is 75.5 percent owned by suburban Chicago-based Sears, the second largest U.S. retailer.
Shares in Sears Mexico and Carso were up strongly on the Mexican Stock Exchange after the announcement.

Sears said it will sell 60 percent of its Sears Mexico stake to Carso for $2.2889 per share. After closing the deal in late April, Carso will offer to buy the remainder of Sears Mexico not owned by Sears at the same price, Sears said.
Still reeling from the 1994-1995 peso devaluation crisis, Sears Mexico has been a small, but persistent problem for its U.S. parent, which these days is focusing on its U.S. market.
"It's going to require additional investment to grow and improve the Mexican business, and with our focus on our core U.S. markets, we decided to seek a Mexican partner," said a Sears spokesmam.
In its latest annual report, Sears said U.S. revenues rose 10.2 percent in 1996 over 1995, while non-U.S. revenues were roughly flat.
"The economic environment continues to be challenging for both Canada and Mexico," Sears said.
Sears said it will post a small charge against earnings on the Carso deal in the first quarter. Analysts said that indicated the Mexican operations were being sold at a loss.
Sears said it will keep a 15 percent interest in Sears Mexico and retain representation on its board of directors.
"The economy in Mexico has not been the greatest over the past few years," said Brown Brothers Harriman retailing analyst Joseph Ronning in New York.

On Monday, Kmart Corp. said it completed the $90 million sale of its share in its Kmart Mexico SA de CV joint venture to Controladora Comercial Mexicana, or Comerci, the second-largest Mexican retailer.
Kmart is the third largest U.S. retailer.
The largest is Wal-Mart Stores Inc., which said in February it will open eight Wal-Mart Supercenters in Mexico this year with its Mexican partner Cifra SA de CV, the largest Mexican retailer.
"Each of these companies is pursuing a different strategy in Mexico," said Merrill Lynch retail analyst Daniel Barry.
Like Sears, Kmart is paring back non-core operations to focus on its U.S. business, analysts said.
Wal-Mart is running out of room to grow at home and sees its long-term future overseas. "Wal-Mart sees international expansion as a major growth strategy," Barry said.
